Archie vs Claude Cowork, Grok Bot, Wix Symphony and Meta Muse.

Their agents work on a computer you rent by the month. Archie works on the one you already own. Everything on this page follows from that.

Archie is in testing. Where it stands → Checked against the sources below on August 20, 2026, September 11 for Symphony, and September 15 for Muse.

The short answer

An agent you own, or an agent you rent.

All five do real work while you are away and hold what matters for your approval. Four of them do it on a computer their company runs, signed into your accounts thereSource 3Source 8Source 16, and bill it as a tier. Archie does it on yours, with the AI billed at cost on an account of your own. Renting buys real things. So does owning.

Renting suits you if

  • You want it working with every computer you own switched off
  • You want a free start that renews every month, which Symphony’s free plan does and our trial does notSource 9
  • You’d rather add an agent to a subscription you already pay for
  • The job needs a browser clicking around arbitrary websites

Owning suits you if

  • You’d rather nothing of yours ran on a computer you can’t see
  • Your account credentials belong in your own password store
  • You want your pick of 7 AI companies, switchable anytime
  • You’d rather pay cost for usage than rent a tier
  • You want advice shaped by your own work rather than by an industry average
Side by side

Owning and renting, row by row.

Archie compared with Claude Cowork, Grok Bot, Wix Symphony and Meta Muse, across whose computer the agent works on, where credentials and files live, where you talk to it, which AI answers, approvals, what happens if the company disappears, and cost

The spread is what renting against owning costs, and Archie’s $30 is the software alone, because the computer is already yours and the thinking is billed at cost on an account of your own.

The AI bill, per piece of work

What one piece of work costs, on their price lists and on ours.

A rented agent sells its AI by the credit, the action or the conversation. Archie’s runs on your own account at the AI company’s price, and we have measured what one reply costs. Each company’s own unit at its own price, with ours beside them.

What one unit of AI work costs on each agent, in that agent’s own unit, from its own price list, beside Archie’s measured cost per reply.
Agent Their unit What it costs
Archie One reply from your agent, with every pass it takes inside it $0.01 when it follows another closely, up to $0.11 when it starts from nothing, measured on an agent with twelve add-ons and everything connected, at BalancedSource 6. A reply that hands work to a specialist or uses the Deep setting costs more. Billed by the AI company to you
Lindy A credit. An “everyday ask” is 2 to 250 of them, “deep work” 250 to 1,000 $29.99 a month for 3,000 credits, so an everyday ask is $0.02 to $2.50 and deep work $2.50 to $10Source 10
Zapier Agents An activity: one action, one search, or one question answered from a knowledge source $400 a year for 1,500 activities a month, about $0.02 eachSource 11
Microsoft Copilot Studio A credit. An answer is 2 of them, an action 5 $200 a month for 25,000 credits, or $0.01 each pay as you go, so a reply that takes two actions is about $0.10 to $0.12Source 12
Salesforce Agentforce A conversation, or an action paid in Flex Credits $2 a conversation, or $0.10 an actionSource 13
Claude Code, an agent on a key like ours A developer’s working day About $13 an active day and $150 to $250 a month, on Anthropic’s own figuresSource 14

Read each row in its own unit: a Lindy credit, a Copilot credit and a reply are different sizes of work, and the companies say so. Ours is one reply with everything it did inside it; most of theirs is one step. Claude Code is a coding agent, which works a problem far harder than an assistant does, and it is here because it is the same kind of bill as ours: an agent on your own key, priced by the AI company. One published three-month log of OpenClaw, another agent on a key, came to $187, $94 and $78 a month as its owner moved to cheaper modelsSource 15. Their figures were read from their own pages on September 12, 2026; ours were measured in August and priced at Anthropic’s rates of September 12. We keep working on ours, and we do not publish how.

Where owning wins

Five things you keep when the agent is yours.

None of these is a setting, and none of them is for rent.

Nothing of yours runs on a computer you cannot see

The agent works on your computer, signed into your accounts there, with the tokens in your computer’s own password store. No server of ours holds your conversations, your files or your sessions, and no rented computer somewhere stays signed in as youSource 5.

You choose the mind, and you can change it

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, xAI, DeepSeek or Mistral, on your own account, switchable whenever you likeSource 5. Pick Anthropic or xAI and the intelligence is the same one behind Cowork or a Grok Bot. The difference is whose computer it is on.

You pay cost, you set the cap, and nothing runs out

The AI company bills you at its own price, on a meter you watch, with a hard cap you set on their dashboard. A reply from a fully loaded agent is $0.01 to $0.11, and a heavier month costs more rather than stoppingSource 6.

Archie asks first, and the gate cannot be switched off

A calendar change is proposed and applied only after you approve it in a later message. An email reply is a draft until you send it. Neither is a setting anyone can turn offSource 5.

Archie outlives us

Our Terms require a final build that needs no license check if we ever stop, so the agent you set up stays yoursSource 7.

Where renting wins

Five things the rent buys.

All five are real, and none of them is going away.

A rented agent runs while everything you own is off

Their agent works from a computer they keep on, so your laptop can be shut, lost, or at the bottom of a bag, and Symphony is built for a phone first, downloaded from an app storeSource 8. Archie works only when your computer does. Shut the lid and it stops until the lid opens; a morning briefing needs the computer awake that morning. That is the honest cost of it living with you rather than with them.

You may already be paying for a rented agent

Cowork is included on the Claude plan a lot of people already have. Adding Archie is a second bill.

You can stay on the free plan

Symphony has a free plan that asks for no card: 500 credits a month and 100 a day, which do not roll overSource 9, and it renews every month. Archie asks for no card either: 14 days on our AI credits, which pass through our server on the way to Anthropic while we are paying, and then free on an AI account of your own at 20 jobs a day, with no end date. A plan takes the limit off at $30 a monthSource 6. The difference from theirs is who pays for the thinking: ours asks you to open an account with an AI company and pay them directly.

A rented agent gets a browser

Cowork can open Chrome and work through a website; a Grok Bot has a whole computer with one built in. Archie works through the connections it ships, and a job that means clicking around an arbitrary website is theirs today.

You can start renting today

All three are shipping: one generally available, one in beta, and Symphony live on iOS, Android and the webSource 8. Archie is in testing, and the waitlist hears the day that changes.

Worth saying

Different landlord, and sometimes a different mind.

Anthropic and xAI are 2 of the 7 companies Archie connects to, so against Cowork and a Grok Bot the intelligence on both sides of this page is literally the same. The choice there is not a smarter agent or a dumber one. It is that a rented computer stays signed into your accounts somewhere you cannot unplug, and the one on your desk, you can.

Symphony is the exception, and it is the more interesting one. It is “powered by Wix AI”Source 8 and offers no way to choose otherwise, so which mind answers you is a decision Wix makes once, for everybody. Their pitch for that is being “built on 20 years of real business expertise”Source 8, drawn from “supporting hundreds of millions of businesses worldwide”Source 8. That is a real thing to offer, and it is worth saying plainly what it is: an average. It knows what businesses like yours tend to do, not what you did last Tuesday or which client is the difficult one. Archie learns the specifics from the files and instructions you give it. Neither is strictly better: one is yours and the other is everybody’s.

You now have every side of that trade, priced.

Sources for every figure and claim on this page
1Claude Cowork, on paid Claude plans

Anthropic’s pricing page, claude.com/pricing, lists “Includes Claude Cowork” on the Pro card, $20 a month or $17 billed annually, read on August 20, 2026. The permission modes, including Skip (“Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”), are in Anthropic’s own guide.

2Where Cowork runs

“Claude’s work runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account.” From Anthropic’s getting-started guide, read on August 20, 2026, which also lists where Cowork is available: the Claude desktop, web and mobile apps.

3Grok Bot

In beta on desktop and iOS; each Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal”, signs in to your tools there, keeps “working 24/7”, and comes back “when something needs your approval”. From xAI’s announcement and its documentation, read on August 20, 2026.

4Grok Bot’s prices

SuperGrok Heavy at $300 a month and Cursor Ultra at $200 a month, from the Grok Bot plan cards, read in a browser and transcribed on August 20, 2026: xAI’s pages refuse automated requests, so this is the one set of figures here no script of ours can re-check. The same cards list Cursor Teams Premium at $120 a seat.

5Archie’s side of the table

The custody claim, the password-store claim, the 7 providers, the 5 chat apps, and the approval gate that cannot be turned off are all on our Trust page, each pointing at the code that makes it true, with instructions for watching the traffic yourself.

6Archie, $30 a month, and the $1 to $5

Our own price, and our own measured figure for light AI use (a handful of tasks a day), both broken down on the pricing page. Heavier use costs more; the meter is yours to watch and cap.

7The final-build commitment

Our Terms require us to publish a version that needs no license check if we cease operating. The wording is in the Terms of Service and the reasoning is on the Trust page.

8Symphony by Wix, and where it runs

An AI agent platform for small businesses with a “mobile-first interface”. “Symphony is available on iOS and Android. Download the app and take your business with you wherever you go”, and it runs in a browser too; you use it with a Wix account, though it needs no Wix website. It is “powered by Wix AI and built on 20 years of real business expertise”, and the page names no model and offers no model choice. Wix does not publish where the agents run, so neither do we: we say how you reach it, which is what their pages state. From wix.com/symphony and the Symphony overview, read on September 11, 2026.

9Symphony’s prices and its credits

Free, then Basic at $16 a month ($12.80 billed annually), Pro at $40 ($32) and Max at $80 ($64). The free plan needs no credit card and carries 500 monthly credits and 100 daily credits; credits “reset monthly and do not roll over”. Basic carries 2,000 monthly credits and Pro 5,000; Max publishes no figure. The unit is defined on the page as: “Each action you take with agents and tools consumes AI credits. The exact amount is calculated after each action, based on its complexity and the tool used.” From wix.com/symphony/pricing, read on September 11, 2026. The daily cap was 50 when this page was first written and is 100 now, so the figure above is the one re-read on that date.

10Lindy’s credits

Plus at $29.99 a month per user with “3k credits / user / mo”, from lindy.ai/pricing, and the ranges “Everyday Asks 2-250 Credits” and “Deep work 250-1,000 Credits” from the same page, read September 12, 2026. The per-ask dollars are our arithmetic on those two published numbers: $29.99 over 3,000 credits is a cent a credit. Lindy’s credits guide adds that “Most teams never come close to their limit.”

11Zapier Agents’ activities

“Agents Pro $400 billed annually” with “up to 1,500 times per month”, from zapier.com/l/agents-pricing, read September 12, 2026. What counts as one activity is from Zapier’s help article: a trigger, an action, a search, a question answered from a knowledge source, each one activity. $400 over twelve months of 1,500 is 2.2 cents, our arithmetic.

12Microsoft Copilot Studio’s credits

“1 capacity pack = 25,000 Copilot Credits” at “$200 per credit pack/month (billed annually)” from Microsoft’s pricing page, and the rate table, generative answer 2 credits and agent action 5, with the pay-as-you-go rate of $0.01 a credit, from Microsoft Learn, both read September 12, 2026. A reply that takes two actions is 12 credits, our arithmetic: $0.096 prepaid, $0.12 metered.

13Salesforce Agentforce’s conversations and actions

“$2 USD per conversation” and “$500 USD per 100,000 Credits” from salesforce.com/agentforce/pricing, and “One Agentforce action consumes 20 Flex Credits ($0.10 USD)” from Salesforce’s Flex Credits announcement, read September 12, 2026.

14What Claude Code costs, in Anthropic’s words

“Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month”, from code.claude.com/docs/en/costs, read September 12, 2026. A coding agent, not an assistant, and on the page for the shape of the bill rather than the size of the job.

15One person’s OpenClaw bill, three months running

A self-hosted OpenClaw agent tracked by its owner: “Month one: $187” on Claude Opus, $94 in month two after moving to Sonnet, $78 in month three, from a dev.to post of March 30, 2026, read September 12, 2026. One log, not a price list, and the only kind of figure that exists for an open-source runner with no price of its own.

16Muse by Meta, and where it runs

Meta’s personal AI agent, announced on September 8, 2026. It “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”, and is “rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai, and coming soon to AI glasses”. It is powered by “Muse Spark, Meta’s most capable model to date”, and the announcement offers no model choice. On approval, in Meta’s words: “Muse checks with the person before sensitive actions like sending an email or making a purchase.” On privacy it says Muse “doesn’t share a person’s conversations or the data in their VM with Meta’s ad systems” and that people “can opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta’s AI models”. On price it says only that Muse is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”: Meta publishes no figure we could read, so we print none. From Meta’s announcement, read on September 15, 2026.

What we have not claimed

Nothing here says these products are careless with your content: each company documents its own isolation, defaults and approvals, and we quote them doing it. The claim is only that their agent works on a computer they run and Archie works on yours. Nothing here says Symphony trains on one customer’s data to answer another, either: we quote what Wix says its intelligence is drawn from and argue about what an average can and cannot know, which is a different point. Each company’s own security documentation is the place to judge their side properly.
